scenes.title: Watch the whole motion first

beats.text: Consider two particles, P and Q, joined by a light string over a small smooth pulley. P is heavier. Both hang at rest.
We let go. P falls, and because the string cannot stretch, Q rises by exactly the same amount.
Then P hits the floor and stops. The string goes slack: nothing pulls Q up any more.
Q is still moving upwards. Gravity slows it, until it stops for an instant at its highest point.
Then it falls back. Two stages: connected, then free.

scenes.title: One acceleration, one tension

beats.text: Why the same acceleration? The string is inextensible: every centimetre P drops, Q rises one centimetre. Same distance, same speed, same acceleration... in opposite directions.
beats.caption: Same a, opposite directions

beats.text: Why the same tension? The string is light and the pulley is smooth, so nothing can change the pull along it. One T, pulling each particle towards the pulley.
beats.caption: One T on both sides

beats.text: If the pulley were rough, friction there could make the two tensions differ. That is why the question says smooth.
beats.caption: Rough pulley: tensions would differ

scenes.title: The whole question

beats.text: Here is the full question. P has mass six kilograms, and Q has mass four kilograms.
P hangs one metre above the floor. Q hangs zero point six metres above the floor.
Light inextensible string, small smooth pulley, released from rest. g is ten metres per second squared.
Assume P stays on the floor when it lands, Q never reaches the pulley, and no air resistance.
Find the acceleration and tension while the string is taut, the speed of P as it hits the floor, and the greatest height Q reaches.
Before any maths: which way does it move? P is heavier, so P goes down and Q up. Take a moment.

scenes.title: Newton’s second law, one particle at a time

beats.text: Isolate P. Down is positive for P, the way it moves. Weight m g pulls down, tension T pulls up.
Newton’s second law: force equals mass times acceleration.
For P, downwards: m g minus T equals m a.
Six times ten is sixty: sixty minus T equals six a.
Now Q. Up is positive for Q. Tension T pulls up, weight m g pulls down.
For Q, upwards: T minus m g equals m a.
Four times ten is forty. T minus forty equals four a.
Add the equations. The T’s cancel: twenty equals ten a.
So the acceleration is two metres per second squared: P down at two, Q up at two.
Put a back into Q’s equation. T equals forty plus four times two: forty-eight newtons, between the two weights.

scenes.title: Stage one: connected motion

beats.text: Stage one, the connected motion. P falls one metre to the floor, so Q rises one metre at the same speed.
Constant acceleration: v squared equals u squared plus two a s.
u is zero, a is two, and s is one. v squared equals zero plus two times two times one.
That is four.
So v is two metres per second, for P hitting the floor and for Q at that same instant.
Where is Q now? It started at zero point six metres and rose one metre: one point six metres above the floor.

scenes.title: Stage two: Q on its own

beats.text: Stage two. P is on the floor, the string is slack, so the tension is zero. Q is on its own.
The only force on Q is its weight. Up is positive, so its acceleration is minus g, minus ten.
Q starts stage two at the speed stage one ended with: u equals two. At the top, v equals zero.
Again, v squared equals u squared plus two a s.
Zero equals four minus twenty s.
So s is zero point two metres more, after the string goes slack.
Greatest height: one point six plus zero point two, which is one point eight metres above the floor.

scenes.title: What if the masses were equal?

beats.text: What would change if P and Q had equal masses? Take a moment.
Nothing moves. The tension equals each weight and the acceleration is zero. The difference in weight drives the motion.
Why both particles share one acceleration and one tension.
